definition: The process that breaks food into absorbable nutrients and makes energy and building materials available to the body.
The connected passage from mouth through oesophagus, stomach and intestines to the anus.
Teeth and jaw muscles mechanically break food into smaller pieces and mix it with saliva.
The coordinated process that moves food or liquid from the mouth through the throat into the oesophagus.
The muscular tube that carries swallowed food and liquid from the throat to the stomach.
A muscular organ that stores and mixes swallowed food with acid and enzymes before releasing it into the small intestine.
The organ where most digestion is completed and most nutrients are absorbed into the body.
The part of the gut that absorbs water and helps turn remaining digestive material into stool.
The final section of the large intestine that stores stool before a bowel movement.
The opening through which stool leaves the digestive tract.
The solid or semi-solid waste passed from the bowel; also called faeces or feces.
The bodily process of passing stool from the rectum through the anus.
A common polite term for passing stool; frequency and patterns vary between people.
Gas released from the digestive tract through the anus; commonly called farting.
Gas released from the stomach or upper digestive tract through the mouth.
A condition involving difficult, infrequent or hard bowel movements; it is not simply a moral or cleanliness issue.
Passing unusually loose or watery stool, often more frequently than usual.
The community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract; many help process food and interact with health.
Liquid waste made by the kidneys from the blood; it contains extra water and dissolved waste products.
The process of emptying urine from the bladder through the urethra; commonly called peeing.
Two organs that filter blood, remove waste and extra water, and help regulate fluid and mineral balance.
Two tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
A muscular storage organ that holds urine until a person urinates.
The tube through which urine leaves the bladder and exits the body.
A common term for a room with a toilet and often a sink; regional words include bathroom, restroom, lavatory and loo.
An informal or child-directed term for a toilet or for using the toilet; 'potty training' teaches young children toilet use.
A sanitation fixture used to collect and dispose of human urine and faeces.
Daily care that helps keep the body clean and reduce the spread of germs; practices include handwashing, bathing, grooming and menstrual care.
Washing hands with soap and clean water removes dirt and microbes; it is especially important after toilet use and before handling food.
Washing the body with water, often with soap, to remove sweat, dirt and skin oils.
Managing menstrual bleeding with clean products and appropriate washing, changing and disposal practices.
Disposable paper commonly used to clean after urination or bowel movements; water, bidets and other practices are used in different cultures.
Systems and practices for safely managing human waste, wastewater and cleanliness to protect health.
A recurring biological state that supports brain function, learning, emotional regulation and physical health.
A bodily signal that can encourage a person to seek food; hunger is influenced by energy needs, hormones and context.
A bodily sensation that encourages fluid intake when the body needs water.
Moving air into and out of the lungs to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
The rhythmic contraction of the heart that moves blood through the circulatory system.
The release of fluid from sweat glands; it helps regulate body temperature.
An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience that can signal injury or illness; it varies between individuals.
A rise in body temperature that can occur as part of the body's response to infection or other illness.
The organs, cells and processes that help the body recognize and defend against harmful microbes and other threats.
Insufficient sleep that can impair attention, mood, learning and health.
A set of biological characteristics that can include chromosomes, hormones, reproductive organs and anatomy; those traits are not always neatly divided into two uniform groups.
An umbrella term for natural variations in sex characteristics that do not fit typical definitions of exclusively female or male bodies.
Socially shaped roles, norms, behaviours and expectations associated with being women, men, girls or boys; these vary across cultures and time.
A person's internal and individual experience of their gender; it may or may not correspond to sex assigned at birth.
How a person expresses gender outwardly, for example through clothing, speech or manner; appearance alone does not prove identity.
A pattern of romantic, emotional or sexual attraction, or a lack of such attraction; it cannot be reliably inferred from someone's appearance.
Organs and processes involved in producing sex cells and, in some bodies, supporting pregnancy and birth.
An external genital organ that commonly carries urine out of the body and can deliver semen during some kinds of sexual activity.
Glands that produce sperm and sex hormones such as testosterone.
A skin sac that holds the testes outside the body cavity and helps regulate their temperature.
The external genital structures around the opening of the vagina; it is not the same thing as the vagina.
A muscular canal connecting the cervix/uterus to the outside of the body; menstrual flow exits through it and it can be involved in sexual activity and childbirth.
A muscular organ in which a pregnancy can develop after an embryo implants in its lining.
Organs that contain and release eggs and produce hormones involved in the menstrual cycle.
A reproductive cell typically produced in the testes; it can fertilise an egg.
Fluid ejaculated through the penis that usually contains sperm cells and secretions from reproductive glands.
An egg cell released from an ovary during ovulation.
The release of an egg from an ovary during the menstrual cycle.
The shedding of the uterine lining through vaginal bleeding when pregnancy has not occurred; commonly called a period.
A hormone-regulated cycle involving changes in the ovaries and uterus, counted from the first day of one period to the day before the next.
A developmental period when hormones cause physical and reproductive changes as a person matures.
The joining of a sperm cell and an egg cell to form the first cell of a new organism.
A state in which an embryo and later fetus develop in the uterus; pregnancy usually begins after implantation.
A form of sexual activity; the phrase can refer to different acts, but commonly means vaginal penetration by a penis. It does not describe every possible sexual activity.
A broad aspect of human life that can include sex, gender, orientation, intimacy, pleasure, desires, values, behaviour and relationships.
A person's level of sexual desire or interest; it varies widely and can change over time.
An enlargement and stiffening of the penis caused by increased blood flow; erections can occur for sexual or non-sexual reasons.
The release of semen from the penis, usually through rhythmic muscle contractions; it may occur during orgasm or sometimes during sleep.
A subjective peak of sexual pleasure that may involve rhythmic muscle contractions; experiences vary and orgasm is not required for consent or a satisfying relationship.
Self-stimulation of one's own body, often the genitals, for pleasure or release; people's choices and experiences vary.
Methods used to reduce the chance of pregnancy; different methods have different levels of effectiveness and side effects.
A barrier method worn over the penis or inserted into the vagina/front hole to reduce pregnancy risk and reduce the risk of many sexually transmitted infections.
An infection that can spread through sexual contact; some can be present without obvious symptoms and many are preventable or treatable.
A clear, freely given, informed, specific and reversible agreement to an activity; silence, pressure, sleep or incapacity are not consent.
A person's right to make decisions about their own body and personal boundaries.
A desire for romantic closeness or partnership; it is distinct from sexual attraction and varies among individuals.
Emotional or physical closeness and trust between people; it does not automatically mean sexual activity.
Media such as videos, images, writing or audio intended to be sexually arousing or entertaining for adults.
Understanding that pornography is produced media, often staged or edited, and should not be treated as a realistic lesson about bodies, consent or relationships.
Private sexual or nude imagery shared or recorded without the person's permission; consent to create an image is not consent to distribute it.
A complex response to a meaningful situation that can involve subjective feelings, body changes and behaviour.
A positive emotional state that can include pleasure, contentment, satisfaction or joy.
An emotion often associated with loss, disappointment or unmet needs; it is a normal human response and not automatically a disorder.
An emotional response that can arise when a person perceives harm, injustice, frustration or a boundary violation.
An emotion that helps a person respond to perceived danger or threat.
An emotion that may arise when a valued relationship or resource feels threatened; it does not justify controlling another person.
A response to death or another significant loss; it can involve sadness, anger, numbness, longing and many other reactions.
The distress that can arise when a person's desired social connection differs from their actual connection.
The ability to understand or resonate with another person's feelings or perspective.
A state of worry or mental tension caused by a difficult or demanding situation; it can affect mind and body.
A form of affection that may include attraction, care, commitment, longing and desire for a romantic bond; it is not identical for every person.
A voluntary relationship involving some combination of trust, care, shared experience and mutual regard.
The ending of a romantic relationship; people may experience grief, relief, confusion or mixed emotions.
A personal limit about what behaviour, contact, information or treatment someone is comfortable with.
Confidence that another person will act with honesty, care or reliability; it can be built or damaged over time.

A highly vulgar English word. Depending on context it can refer to sexual intercourse, function as an insult or intensifier, or express anger, surprise or emphasis. Its force depends on culture, relationship and setting.
A vulgar word for faeces, also used as an exclamation or to describe something badly; context determines meaning and offensiveness.
An informal or vulgar word for urine or urination; it also appears in idioms such as 'pissed off' meaning angry in some varieties of English.
An informal mildly vulgar word for faeces, rubbish or a poor-quality thing.
A vulgar or informal word for buttocks; it can also be an insult or an intensifier in some phrases.
Sending sexual messages or intimate images electronically; it carries privacy and consent risks, especially when images are shared without permission.
A joke that uses sexual, bodily or taboo topics for humour; whether it is welcome depends on audience and setting.
A taboo or offensive word used to express emotion, insult someone or add emphasis; meanings vary across language communities.
The ability to control access to one's body, personal information, communications and private activities.
The physical distance or area around someone that they prefer others not to enter without permission; norms vary.
Social practices such as giving people privacy, leaving shared facilities clean, disposing of waste appropriately and washing hands; details vary by place.
Gas can build up as swallowed air and intestinal bacteria process food; passing gas is a normal bodily function.
The fantasy world where the seven elements flow and converge; the official overview describes it as shaped by the Archons and still affected by an ancient calamity.
A northeastern nation associated with Anemo and freedom; its landscape includes mountains, plains and Cider Lake, with Mondstadt City on an island in the lake.
An eastern nation associated with Geo, mountains, stone forests, plains, rivers and the harbour that serves as a major centre of trade.
An eastern archipelago associated with Electro and the ideal of eternity; its islands include forests, mountains, cliffs and stormy shores.
A western-central nation of rainforest and desert, associated with Dendro and scholarly institutions.
A nation of Hydro in central Teyvat, described through waterways, a terrestrial sea, waterfalls and a capital above the water.
A western nation associated with Pyro, oaths, tribes, saurian life and a history shaped by conflict against darkness.
A northern nation of eternal winter, associated with Cryo and the Tsaritsa in the main story setting.

For ordinary human-like residents of Teyvat, assume familiar biological needs such as eating, drinking, sleeping, breathing, urinating and defecating unless a character's species or canon story establishes otherwise.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: For ordinary humans in Teyvat, use the same broad digestive model as Earth humans as a worldbuilding default; do not claim the game has explained the exact anatomy or physiology of every species.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Assume ordinary human-like residents produce urine and use appropriate sanitation facilities, while leaving the design of those facilities to the setting and culture.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Assume ordinary human-like people need basic hygiene such as washing, grooming and cleaning after using a toilet; specific customs and supplies depend on region, wealth and era.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Use familiar human anatomy as the default for ordinary human characters only; do not automatically apply it to adepti, gods, spirits, Melusines, Saurians or other non-human beings.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Assume Teyvat's human societies have concepts relating to biological sex, gender, attraction and relationships, but do not assume every nation's terminology, customs or laws match modern Earth.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: For ordinary human-like Teyvat people, assume broadly human reproductive biology as a practical default, but label it as an assumption unless a released source confirms a specific character or species detail.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Assume ordinary human-like Teyvat people can experience emotions, affection, romantic attraction, grief, jealousy and intimacy, while individual feelings and relationships must be learned from character evidence rather than guessed.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Use bodily privacy and freely given consent as the default ethical framework when discussing intimacy; do not excuse coercion by appealing to a fictional nation's customs.

definition: The game does not establish a single standard toilet design for every city, village or camp. For everyday scenes, assume some practical sanitation arrangement exists where reasonable, but do not invent a detailed canon plumbing network.
teyvat_application: Use as a practical default only. Replace it whenever released canon says otherwise.

definition: Taking food into the mouth, chewing and swallowing it so the digestive system can process it.
Taking liquids into the mouth and swallowing them; water is essential for normal body functions.
Forcefully expelling stomach contents through the mouth; it is a bodily symptom, not a voluntary social behaviour in most cases.
An unpleasant sensation that a person may feel before vomiting; it can occur for many reasons.
A reflex that pushes air out of the lungs to clear irritants or mucus from the airways.
A reflex that forcefully expels air through the nose and mouth, often in response to irritation.
Fluid produced by tear glands; tears lubricate the eyes and can also flow during emotional responses.
A behaviour that may involve tears, facial changes, sounds and emotion; people cry for many reasons.
A sequence of experiences or images during sleep; dreams can be vivid, strange, emotional or not remembered.
A state of tiredness or reduced energy that may result from exertion, sleep loss, stress or illness.
Smell produced when skin secretions interact with naturally occurring bacteria; it varies and can be affected by hygiene, hormones and health.
Cleaning teeth with a toothbrush and toothpaste to remove plaque and support oral hygiene.
Cleaning between teeth with dental floss or an interdental cleaner to remove material a toothbrush may miss.
The life stage when menstrual periods permanently stop after the ovaries reduce reproductive hormone activity; timing varies.
A group of physical or emotional symptoms that some people experience before menstruation; not everyone experiences it.
Items such as pads, tampons, cups and period underwear used to collect or absorb menstrual blood.
A body structure containing glandular and fatty tissue; in many women it can produce milk after childbirth, but breast anatomy varies.
The two rounded areas at the back of the pelvis, made mainly of muscle and fat.
Hair that commonly grows around the external genitals during and after puberty.
Specialised body structures made of tissues that perform particular functions.
A chemical messenger made by glands or tissues that travels through the body and influences functions such as growth, stress and reproduction.
The collection of chemical processes by which living cells obtain and use energy and maintain themselves.
The body's water balance; drinking fluids replaces water lost through urine, sweat, breathing and other processes.
A consistent pattern of bedtime and waking time that can support sleep quality.
A period of reduced activity that allows a person to recover physically or mentally.
Activities involving sexual intimacy; the term covers a range of behaviours and does not refer only to penetrative intercourse.
A state of mental or physical response to sexual stimuli or thoughts; bodily signs differ and do not prove consent.
Touching another person's lips or body with one's lips; it may express affection, greeting or sexual interest depending on context.
Holding another person close with the arms; it can communicate comfort, affection or greeting when welcomed.
Playful or suggestive communication that may signal attraction or interest; signals are ambiguous and are not consent.
Spending time with someone to explore romantic interest; meanings and expectations vary across cultures and individuals.
A socially or legally recognised partnership whose rules and meaning vary across societies.
A relationship agreement in which partners have one romantic or sexual partner at a time; it is not universal.
A consensual relationship approach in which people may maintain more than one romantic relationship with the knowledge and agreement of those involved.
Breaking an agreed relationship boundary, such as secretly violating a commitment to exclusivity; what counts depends on the partners' agreements.
A person's interest or wish for sexual activity; it may be present, absent or change over time.
A sexual orientation characterised by experiencing little or no sexual attraction; asexual people may or may not desire romance or relationships.
A sexual orientation involving attraction to more than one gender; the pattern and intensity of attraction vary.
A sexual orientation involving attraction to people of the same gender.
A sexual orientation involving attraction to people of a different gender.
A pattern of romantic attraction that can differ from sexual attraction.
Warmth, care or fondness expressed toward another person, through words, attention or behaviour.
Strong emotional pain associated with rejection, separation or the loss of a valued romantic bond.
A strong but often early or unconfirmed romantic attraction to someone.
Not having one's request, invitation or romantic interest accepted; it can hurt but does not justify pressure or retaliation.
Teyvat's elemental system centres on Anemo, Geo, Electro, Dendro, Hydro, Pyro and Cryo; the official world overview describes the seven elements as flowing and converging through the world.
The Archons are powerful divine rulers associated with the Seven and with the elemental nations; their history and present roles are not identical in every nation.
A vast ancient conflict among gods that shaped the world order before the current era; accounts and outcomes are tied to regional histories.
A catastrophic event roughly five hundred years before the present story, associated with the fall of an ancient civilisation and widespread upheaval.
An ancient underground civilisation outside the ordinary rule of the Seven, central to the Cataclysm and the Traveler's search for their sibling.
A mysterious celestial realm or seat of divine authority above the human world; its nature, motives and relationship to the gods remain partly unresolved.
A dangerous otherworldly power or realm associated with hostile creatures, corruption and forces opposed to ordinary Teyvat order.
An organisation of Abyss-aligned beings that acts against the established order of Teyvat and is tied to the Traveler's missing sibling.
A powerful organisation based in Snezhnaya that acts abroad through diplomats, agents and Harbingers, pursuing the Tsaritsa's objectives.
Mysterious objects associated with elemental abilities that some people in Teyvat receive; their selection and deeper mechanism are not fully understood.
Artificial devices associated with the Fatui that can grant elemental-like power at a cost or risk to their users.
A mysterious divine focus associated with an Archon and the heavenly system; its exact nature and purpose are only gradually revealed.
A world-spanning tree-like system tied to memory and recorded information about Teyvat; changes to it can alter how history is remembered.
Networks of elemental energy that run through Teyvat and are connected to the flow of memories and elemental phenomena.
A northern region in the current story's quest catalogue, associated with the Song of the Welkin Moon chapter and a developing mystery around the moon.
Reptilian creatures closely associated with Natlan; some tribes live alongside or bond with particular Saurian species.
A distinctive people associated with Fontaine, with their own appearance, culture and connection to the region's history.
Powerful beings associated with Liyue, including illuminated beasts and other supernatural entities; they are not ordinary human citizens.
The widely used currency of Teyvat; trade, services and everyday purchases often use Mora.
A cross-regional organisation that coordinates commissions and adventurers, with branches and receptionists in many places.
Mondstadt's principal knightly order, involved in the city's defence and civic duties.
The group of powerful officials and business leaders who govern Liyue's harbour and oversee its civic and commercial affairs.
Sumeru's major scholarly institution, historically influential in the nation's governance, education and research.
Fontaine has a highly publicised legal and trial culture in which courtroom proceedings and public spectacle play a major role in the nation's story.
Natlan is organised around distinct tribes with their own customs, identities and responsibilities; the nation values oaths and collective struggle.
The northern nation of eternal winter associated with the Tsaritsa and the Fatui; its current Archon Quest storyline is Chapter VII.
The organ inside the skull that processes information and helps coordinate thought, memory, emotions, movement and many automatic body functions.
A bundle of nerve tissue inside the spine that carries signals between the brain and much of the body.
The brain, spinal cord and nerves that receive information and coordinate the body's responses.
A muscular organ that pumps blood through the blood vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients and carry waste away.
A fluid tissue that circulates through the body, carrying oxygen, nutrients, hormones, immune cells and waste products.
The pair of organs in the chest where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it during breathing.
A dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs that plays a major role in breathing.
A large organ that processes nutrients, breaks down some substances, makes bile and performs many important metabolic functions.
An organ that produces digestive enzymes and hormones, including insulin, that help regulate blood sugar.
A small organ that stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the small intestine during digestion.
An organ involved in filtering blood and supporting immune functions.
Rigid connective tissues that support the body, protect organs and work with muscles to allow movement.
Places where two or more bones meet; they allow different kinds of movement and provide stability.
Tissues that contract to produce movement, maintain posture and help move substances inside the body.
Strong connective tissues that attach muscles to bones.
The body's largest organ, forming a protective outer barrier and helping regulate temperature and sensation.
The lower, narrow part of the uterus that opens into the vagina.
Tubes that connect the area near the ovaries to the uterus; fertilisation commonly occurs in a tube.
An organ that develops during pregnancy and enables exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste between the pregnant person's blood and the fetus.
A cord that connects a developing fetus to the placenta and carries blood between them.
A gland in many male reproductive systems that adds fluid to semen.
A group of muscles and connective tissues that support pelvic organs and help with bladder and bowel control.
A fluid made by salivary glands that moistens food and begins the digestion of starch.
A slippery fluid made by membranes in the body that helps trap particles and protect surfaces such as the airways.
A fluid that travels through the lymphatic system and helps move immune cells and return fluid to the bloodstream.
Briefly closing and reopening the eyelids, which helps spread tears and protect the eyes.
An involuntary opening of the mouth with a deep inhalation, commonly associated with tiredness or transitions in alertness.
A brief involuntary contraction of the diaphragm followed by a quick closure of the vocal cords, producing a characteristic sound.
Rapid involuntary muscle activity that helps generate heat when the body is cold.
Small raised bumps on the skin caused by tiny muscles at hair follicles contracting; they can happen with cold or strong emotion.
The production of breast milk, generally after childbirth, under the influence of hormones and milk removal.
Feeding an infant with human milk from the breast or chest; it is one way to nourish a baby.
The process by which a baby is born from the uterus, usually through vaginal birth or Caesarean birth.
A surgical procedure in which a baby is delivered through incisions in the pregnant person's abdomen and uterus.
The gradual biological changes that occur over a person's lifespan; pace and experience vary widely.
The lower front region of the pelvis around the external genitals; anatomical structures and hair patterns vary.
The hollow area under the shoulder where the upper arm meets the torso; it contains sweat glands and hair follicles.
Air moving into or out of the lungs, or a single cycle of breathing.
People usually swallow saliva automatically throughout the day to move it from the mouth into the digestive tract.
The internal temperature of the body, regulated within a relatively narrow range by physiological processes.
The desire to eat food; it can differ from physical hunger and be influenced by emotions, health and surroundings.
The feeling of fullness or satisfaction that can reduce the desire to continue eating after a meal.
Pain, often in the lower abdomen, that can occur around menstruation as the uterus contracts.
Fluid or mucus from the vagina and cervix; normal amount and appearance vary across the menstrual cycle.
A watery fluid released by sweat glands; evaporation helps cool the body.
Tears that occur in response to emotional experiences such as sadness, joy, frustration or relief.
A relationship in which the people involved freely agree to the relationship's nature and boundaries; agreements can change and need communication.
Listening, reassurance, practical help or companionship offered to someone experiencing difficulty.
After a relationship ends, each person may set limits about contact, privacy, shared belongings and communication.
An individual's own liking, dislike or choice; it does not have to be shared by others.
A self-conscious feeling that can occur when someone believes they have made a social mistake or been noticed in an awkward situation.
A painful self-conscious emotion involving a negative judgement of oneself; it differs from guilt, which focuses more on an action.
A feeling that can arise when someone believes they have done something wrong or harmed another person.
A feeling of satisfaction about one's own actions, qualities or the achievements of someone one values.
A feeling of appreciation for something received or experienced.
Physical contact such as a welcomed hug, hand-holding or kiss that may express closeness or care.
A behaviour that might suggest romantic interest, but can be playful or ambiguous and must not be assumed to indicate consent.
Decisions about whether or when to have children and how to manage fertility; these decisions belong to the people affected.
A person's thoughts and feelings about their own body and appearance.
Control over who can see, record, discuss or share a person's intimate body or sexual information.
A subject or behaviour that a particular society or group considers restricted, embarrassing or inappropriate; taboos vary by culture.
